Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

The name identifies locations discussed in Israel’s history, including references associated with Judah, Benjamin, and the reign of Saul. Its precise significance in any passage depends on which Gibeah and surrounding events the context identifies.

Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal sense identifies a female superior or head of a household relationship.

e.t: “Doeg” is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the name occurs eight times, all in four verses in 1 Samuel 21–22. Its recorded uses connect Doeg with spoken exchanges and with events involving death, so it functions as the identifying name of a person in the narrative. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain his specific actions in any one occurrence.

Dishon is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Dishon.” It identifies individuals named in the genealogical records of Genesis and 1 Chronicles rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across six verses. Because no short definition is provided and its uses are as a name, its ordinary scriptural function is identification within family and descendant lists, not the expression of a broader idea or concept.

Within the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs eight times, all in Genesis 4, where the name is connected with family events and speech. Its normal scriptural use is therefore as a personal designation. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening whenever the name appears.

This Hebrew word means “beauty.” It names the quality of attractiveness or splendor associated with a person, place, or act, depending on the sentence. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Chronicles, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its repeated association with worship language shows that beauty can describe something presented honorably before God, while its use in Proverbs shows that it can also relate to a community’s flourishing. The surrounding verse determines its precise emphasis.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “riches,” referring to accumulated material resources or possessions. It can describe what people possess, exchange, give away, or trust in, so its use reaches beyond money alone to personal or commercial wealth. The word occurs 26 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Proverbs, where riches are considered alongside wisdom, security, justice, and human desire. Its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding context.

Hena is a proper name preserved in English as “Hena.” It functions as a specific designation rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears three times, and each occurrence is rendered “Hena,” showing a consistent name rather than a translated concept. Its references are 2 Kings 18:34, 2 Kings 19:13, and Isaiah 37:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role in each passage.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Zabdi.” It identifies different men in the Old Testament rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. It occurs six times in six verses: three times in Joshua, twice in 1 Chronicles, and once in Nehemiah. In Joshua, the name identifies a man connected with the family line examined after Israel’s sin at Jericho; other occurrences identify men listed in genealogies or community records. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding account, but its ordinary function is simply a man’s name.

This Hebrew word means “sown.” It describes seed or something placed in the ground for growth, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming the person who plants it. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, in Leviticus 11:37 and Isaiah 61:11. Its use connects naturally with the action of sowing and with what comes from that action, so the word points to something that has been planted. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “that” and functions as a connective in Old Testament sentences. It helps link one statement with something already mentioned or with the circumstance being described, rather than naming a person, object, or action. The word occurs 141 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing across historical, poetic, and prophetic books. Its exact role in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its normal function is to point back or connect ideas in the flow of speech.

The word means “wise,” describing people regarded as possessing wisdom or understanding. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 14 times, all in Daniel. The listed references in Daniel 2 show repeated use of this description, while the wider occurrence range extends through Daniel 5. It points to a quality attributed to people, not an action, place, or personal name.

This Hebrew noun means “brothers.” It names or refers to brothers as a group and functions as a noun rather than an action or description. The word itself supplies a family or brotherhood designation, while the sentence determines who is included. In the Hebrew Old Testament data provided here, it occurs twice, both in Ezra 7:18. Because the surrounding verse is not included, the precise reference of “brothers” there must be understood from that passage’s context.

This Hebrew word means “armed,” describing people equipped for action. As used here, it functions as a description of people who are armed. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus, Joshua, and Judges. The word is applied to groups of people, identifying their armed condition. Its repeated use in these passages presents “armed” as the central idea wherever this word occurs.

This Hebrew word is rendered “several” and functions as a noun describing a distinct living arrangement or place. It appears three times in the Old Testament, in two verses: 2 Kings 15:5 and 2 Chronicles 26:21. Its wording is associated with being and dwelling, so it identifies where someone was situated rather than describing an action. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic recorded meaning is “several.”

This word describes something as "waste": left barren, empty, or unproductive rather than flourishing or inhabited. In its eight Old Testament occurrences, it is used of conditions affecting offerings, homes, cities, land, and other places. Its meaning can therefore describe a state of ruin or barrenness, especially when a place has lost its former life or usefulness. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on physical barrenness, abandonment, or ruin.

This Hebrew word describes something as “miry,” expressing the quality conveyed by that English meaning. It functions as a descriptive term, identifying something by its condition rather than naming a person, place, or action. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both in Daniel 2:41 and 2:43. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains the same: “miry.”

This Hebrew word means “before.” It marks something that happens earlier than another event, setting a temporal boundary in the sentence. It can describe what has not happened yet or what occurs prior to a stated action or time. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 57 times, showing regular use for ordering events and circumstances in time. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a reference to what comes earlier.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “dearly,” expressing something regarded with deep personal affection. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Jeremiah 12:7. Its role there is connected with the thing being acted upon, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force of the expression. Thus, the word points to a valued relationship or possession held dearly rather than merely identifying an ordinary object.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “great,” functioning as a descriptive term rather than naming an action. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once each in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its recorded usage consistently points to something described as great. The word appears in Leviticus 11:17, Deuteronomy 14:16, and Isaiah 34:11.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Jerubbaal,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies the same named person throughout its Old Testament use. The name occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, chiefly in Judges and once in 1 Samuel. Its role in a particular passage is therefore to identify that person, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific action or circumstance connected with him.

This Hebrew noun means “grievousness,” expressing something experienced as difficult, oppressive, or weighty. It names a condition or quality rather than an action. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Nahum. Its uses are connected with situations that press heavily upon people, but the precise force in any individual verse depends on that passage’s surrounding words.

This word means “now”. It points to the present time, marking what is happening or being requested at the current moment. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears 13 times, concentrated in Ezra and Daniel. Its use helps anchor a statement in the immediate situation rather than in an earlier or later time. The surrounding passage determines exactly what action, event, or request is being placed in the present.

This Hebrew word describes something as “cruel,” identifying a quality marked by merciless treatment or character. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its meaning is established across several passages rather than being tied to one isolated use. The exact person, creature, or situation described must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. It names a harsh quality wherever it appears.

This Hebrew word refers to “languages,” meaning distinct forms of human speech used by different peoples. It is a plural noun, so it points to more than one language rather than to a single way of speaking. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel, it is used for the languages of various peoples and nations. The word appears from Daniel 3 through Daniel 7, showing a consistent reference to languages within Daniel’s accounts.

Mibzar is the English rendering used for this Hebrew word, which functions as a personal name rather than a translated descriptive term. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Genesis 36:42 and 1 Chronicles 1:53. Because no explicit definition is provided, its ordinary meaning is best represented by the name “Mibzar,” while the surrounding verse determines the person being identified. The word is therefore primarily a name, not a general action, quality, or object.

This Hebrew word refers to a wound or injury—a damaging condition that needs healing or repair. It appears three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in two verses: Jeremiah 30:13 and Hosea 5:13. Its use describes a condition considered in relation to help, treatment, or restoration rather than merely naming an ordinary physical object. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the injury itself or the need for its remedy.

The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Exodus 34:33–35. Its associated actions include giving, removing, and speaking with the veil involved, showing that it functions as a physical covering rather than an action or quality.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “convocation.” It names an assembly called together, especially for an appointed occasion before God. In the Old Testament, it is used for the publicly recognized gatherings connected with Israel’s sacred days and worship. Its use in Exodus and Leviticus shows that the word describes more than an ordinary meeting: it identifies a formally summoned gathering. The word occurs 23 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its role in any particular passage is clarified by that passage’s surrounding instructions.

Meshillemoth is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. Its meaning is preserved in English as “Meshillemoth,” so the name itself identifies the person being mentioned. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 2 Chronicles and once in Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not establish additional meaning or significance beyond identifying its bearer.

This Hebrew word means “lewdness,” naming sexually improper conduct rather than an action someone performs. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Hosea 2:10. Its role is to identify lewdness as the object associated with the conduct described in that passage. The word itself gives the basic category of wrongdoing; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine the precise force of the reference.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “pottage,” referring to a cooked dish. It names food as an object in the sentence rather than an action or description. The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, 2 Kings, and Haggai. Its uses involve pottage being prepared, given, or spoken about, showing a consistent reference to the dish itself. The exact significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

This Hebrew word means “fall” or “fell.” It describes movement downward, whether someone or something drops, collapses, or comes down. It can also express a person falling in defeat or being brought down. The word occurs 435 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it is used broadly for literal falling and related downward movement. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word refers to a “talebearer”: a person who carries reports from one person to another, often spreading information that can stir trouble or deepen conflict. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Proverbs. Its repeated use there presents this kind of speech as something that moves through relationships and affects how people live together. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “down,” describing the act of tearing down, throwing down, or demolishing something. It commonly functions as an action word for removing structures, altars, walls, or other objects from their standing position. The central idea is forcefully bringing something down rather than merely moving it. It occurs 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a repeated use for physical destruction or dismantling. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being brought down.

This Hebrew word means “worship.” It describes the act of bowing before or honoring someone as worthy of reverence. In its biblical use, it functions as an action word: people worship a person or an image, expressing submission or devotion through their response. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, where it repeatedly describes worship directed toward a king or an image. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes something as “thick,” emphasizing substantial depth or density rather than thinness. It appears three times in the Old Testament, in descriptions connected with architectural features in Solomon’s temple and Ezekiel’s temple vision. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description, but its ordinary sense is a physical feature that is thick or substantial.

The name appears 16 times in 14 Old Testament verses, including lists of priests and other family lines. Its repeated use in genealogical settings shows that it functions as an identifying name for particular individuals; the surrounding passage is needed to distinguish which Amariah is intended in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb describes being "overwhelmed"—brought into a condition where a person or thing is overcome or pressed down. It can describe an inward condition as well as something covered or weakened, depending on the sentence. The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including poetry and narrative, so its central idea is broader than one particular situation. Its precise force in any verse comes from the surrounding words and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “yoke,” the device placed on an animal to harness it for work. In the Old Testament, the word can also describe the burdensome rule, labor, or submission imposed on people, using the physical yoke as a picture of imposed obligation. It appears 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about a yoke being placed on a people and about relief from such a burden. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes someone who is “barren,” especially a woman unable to bear children. It is used of reproductive barrenness in the Old Testament, appearing 12 times across 11 verses. The word occurs in accounts involving women who have no children and in statements about freedom from barrenness. Its central sense concerns the inability to produce offspring, while the surrounding passage determines how that condition is being described or addressed.

This word means “meet,” describing people or groups coming together. It functions as an action word, focusing on the meeting itself rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across 14 verses, so its basic sense is established in several settings. The surrounding passage determines whether the meeting is planned, unexpected, friendly, or tense; the word itself centers on the act of meeting.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be determined from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 9:33. No explicit definition, gloss, English rendering, or approved fallback meaning is available, so a more specific translation would go beyond the evidence. Its exact sense must therefore be established from the surrounding verse and passage, rather than from this word record alone.

e.t: This Hebrew word identifies a person associated with Pirathon and is rendered “Pirathonite.” It functions as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word appears five times in the Old Testament, identifying individuals in Judges, Samuel, and Chronicles. Its repeated use shows that “Pirathonite” marks a person’s association with Pirathon across different accounts and periods of Israel’s history.

This Hebrew word means “righteousness,” referring to what is right, just, and morally upright. It functions as a noun, naming a quality or standard of right conduct rather than an action itself. In its one Old Testament occurrence, it is rendered “righteousness” and appears in Daniel 4:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is conduct that accords with what is right before God and others.

This Hebrew verb means “laugh.” It describes the act of laughing or expressing laughter. In the Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, most often in Genesis, and can function as the action performed by a person or group. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation, but the central idea remains the act of laughing rather than a person, object, or place. The word is found from Genesis through Judges.

This Hebrew word functions as a small definite-word marker, commonly rendered “the.” It points to a particular person, thing, or category rather than naming an action or quality itself. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Ezra 4:13. Its precise contribution in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, since the verse text is not included here.

“Zemarite” refers to a member of the Zemarite people. It functions as a group or people-name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew term occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, in Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16. The two occurrences identify the same people-name, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each passage’s particular context.

It is used across the Old Testament for burial places and interment, including family and royal burials. The word occurs 14 times in 13 Old Testament verses, showing a consistent association with death, burial, and the resting place of the dead.

This Hebrew word expresses “for,” functioning in a sentence to identify the action or circumstance being stated. It appears 27 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 27 verses, so its use is repeated but not tied to one setting. As a predicate, it helps connect the subject with what is being expressed. Its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence, while its central lexical meaning remains “for.”

This Hebrew word describes being “on” something, especially in connection with riding or being carried on an animal or vehicle. It functions as an action word describing a person’s position or movement in relation to what carries them. It occurs 78 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages involving people and objects associated with riding. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew verb means “buy”: to obtain something by paying for it. It commonly describes purchasing food or other goods, as in the repeated account of people obtaining grain during famine. The same basic action can involve buying from another person or obtaining needed provisions. It occurs 21 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Genesis and additional uses in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Proverbs, and Amos. Its normal sense is straightforward: securing something through a transaction rather than receiving it freely.

Its precise role can depend on the surrounding sentence, but its normal scriptural setting is the sphere of wisdom and thoughtful guidance.
